demagogue

/DEM-uh-gog/ - the stress falls on DEM · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Demagogue means a leader who gains power by appealing to people's prejudices.

The pamphlet's warning has aged well: a demagogue never argues with figures when a scapegoat stands closer to hand.

Example

In the winter of 1936 the radio priest — the era's great demagogue — drew thirty million listeners a week. Each program opened on a grievance his listeners nursed — lost farms, lost wages — and closed by blaming the same short list: bankers, foreigners, and whoever had doubted him that week. He gave the air no numbers and took no questions, and any station that dropped him joined the list beside the bankers.

Demagogue is the exact word for him because it means a leader who gains power by appealing to people's prejudices — the power grows from stoking suspicions his listeners walked in carrying, not from any case he could defend. A firebrand may burn hot for a cause; the demagogue needs your resentment of somebody else to live on.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

agitator: An agitator stirs discontent on purpose — strikes, marches, unrest — and the cause may even be a just one. A demagogue has no cause but himself: he feeds an audience's prejudices because prejudice, once fed, converts straight into his power.

firebrand: A firebrand burns hot for a cause, honest or not — the heat is real conviction, and there is no scapegoating in it. A demagogue supplies no conviction of his own; his power is built by aiming an audience's prejudice at somebody else.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

statesman: leads by judgment and persuasion, and will lose a crowd rather than hand it a scapegoat

peacemaker: lowers the very temperature the demagogue lives on

Where it sits · how far the audience gets weaponized

crowd-pleaser → rabble-rouser → demagogue

crowd-pleaser vs. demagogue: A crowd-pleaser is far milder than a demagogue: he only flatters with jokes and applause lines, no harm meant, while a demagogue turns the crowd's prejudices into his own power.

rabble-rouser vs. demagogue: A rabble-rouser goes further than a crowd-pleaser — the crowd leaves angry and aimed at someone; the demagogue claims the most: prejudice fed steadily until it hardens into his power.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — dem-: the people (Greek demos)

Root — -agogue: leader (Greek agogos)

Put it together: Dem- (the people) + -agogue (leader) = a leader of the people — and there is no de- prefix anywhere in it. The word is Greek: in Athens a demagogos began as an everyday job description, and centuries of bad examples turned it into an accusation. The same -agogue walks schoolchildren in pedagogue, and the same dem- votes in democracy.

Use the root in a new word: democracy: Democracy joins dem- to -cracy, "rule": rule by the people — the crowd a demagogue courts is the same demos that votes.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / political, always disapproving

Demagogue is an accusation, not a job title — save it for leaders whose power is built on prejudice. A loud, passionate speaker may be only a firebrand; a skilled and honest one, an orator. And note the word's one trick: it wears this unit's de- as a costume. Its dem- is Greek for "the people," cousin to democracy, and nothing in it is lowered or undone.
